A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Himalayan fold–thrust belt is a single thrust sheet with a complex duplex geometry that repeats the Subhimalayan, Lesser Himalayan, and Greater Himalayan sections.

the Himalayan fold-and-thrust belt in Bhutan is characterized by (1) a simple structural architecture, (2) significant crustal shortening, (3) passive duplexing of the overlying Greater and Tethyan units above a roof thrust, (4) a significant component of shortening in the lower crust, and (5) a significant component (31–53 km) of structural overlap across the South Tibetan detachment.
the Himalayan fold–thrust belt of eastern and central (and western) Bhutan is characterized by (1) a relatively simple structural geometry and (2) a relatively low amount of crustal shortening.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Himalayan thrust belt is a continuous, eastward-thinning system that has undergone significant crustal shortening, with a total of 70%–75% shortening in the Himalayan fold–thrust belt and 25%–30% shortening in Tibetan lithosphere.
the crust of the Himalayan orogen is composed of three distinct tectonic units (Subhimalayan, Lesser Himalayan, and Greater Himalayan), each of which is characterized by a different tectonic style.

the Himalaya in Bhutan is an example of a fold-and-thrust belt that is not simply a passive response to convergence, but rather an actively evolving system that has accommodated a significant portion of the convergence between India and Eurasia.
